activities.anchor: the discouraged and retired don't count
activities.caption: fill the blanks — who counts as unemployed
activities.name: ueDefinitionCloze

config.text: The unemployment rate is the number of unemployed divided by the %%0%%. To count as unemployed you must be without work, available to start and %%1%% seeking work in the past four weeks. Reading the rate alongside the %%2%% rate reveals whether the labour force itself is shrinking.
config.hint: The denominator is employed plus unemployed; participation is the labour force as a share of the working-age population.

activities.anchor: The boundary choices create the measurement politics
activities.caption: where does each person sit?
activities.name: ueBoundarySort

config.prompt: Where does each person sit in the labour-market statistics?

items.label: a part-time barista who wants full-time hours
a graduate sending applications this week
a discouraged worker who stopped looking
someone claiming benefits but not actively seeking

config.why: Underemployment is counted as employed, discouraged workers leave the labour force, and benefit claimants can be outside it — three ways the headline misleads.

activities.caption: pair each type with its example and remedy
activities.name: ueTypesMatch

config.prompt: Pair each type of unemployment with its example and remedy:

pairs.right: a graduate searching for a better match — healthy, and helped by better job matching
a coal region whose skills do not fit the new healthcare jobs — retraining and relocation
layoffs in a recession — fiscal and monetary demand policy

config.why: The type determines the remedy: search, matching or demand.

activities.anchor: wages fall until everyone who wants work finds it
activities.caption: how a demand slump becomes layoffs
activities.name: ueStickyOrder

config.prompt: How a demand slump becomes layoffs — put the chain in order:
items: Demand for goods falls and firms need fewer hours
Contracts, morale and fairness norms stop wages falling enough to clear the market
Firms adjust by quantity instead of price
They cut hours, temps and finally headcount
Unemployment rises even though the market could in theory clear at lower pay
config.why: Sticky wages make jobs, not pay, the shock absorber — which is why a demand slump shows up as layoffs.

activities.anchor: if wages simply fell far enough
activities.caption: find the sticky-wage slip
activities.name: ueStickySpot

config.prompt: Find the line where the sticky-wage reasoning goes wrong:
lines: In a frictionless market, a glut of labour clears by cutting wages.
Real firms could do the same, so persistent unemployment must reflect greed or regulation alone.
Yet contracts, morale and fairness norms make pay cuts self-defeating for employers.
Firms therefore adjust by hiring fewer people rather than cutting pay.
That is why jobs, not wages, absorb a demand slump.
config.correction: The obstacle runs deeper than greed or regulation: pay cuts damage morale and retention, so firms cut jobs instead.
config.why: Wages do adjust — slowly — and the puzzle is why they adjust too slowly to stop jobs from absorbing the shock.

activities.anchor: shortfall of real GDP from potential
activities.caption: call the Okun output gap
activities.name: ueOkunEst

config.prompt: Actual unemployment is 6% and the natural rate is 4%. Using Okun's rule of roughly 2% of GDP per point, what is the estimated output gap?
config.why: Two points above the natural rate × 2% per point = about 4% of GDP below potential. The coefficient varies: nearer 1–1.5 where hours adjust before headcount.
config.context: a sizing rule, not a mechanism

activities.anchor: measured what import competition from China did
activities.caption: diagnose a coal region — and pick the policy
activities.name: ueChinaBranch

config.root: A coal-mining region stays depressed for a decade after the pits close; the new jobs are in healthcare, in another city, and need different skills. Trace the diagnosis and the policy.

start.text: Which type of unemployment is this?

choices.label: Structural — a skills-and-location mismatch
choices.feedback: Yes — the signature is long duration and mismatch, not a lack of demand.

choices.label: Cyclical — the recession share
choices.feedback: Demand policy cannot move a miner into a healthcare job in another city.

choices.label: Frictional — normal search
choices.feedback: Search takes weeks; this has lasted a decade.

choices.label: Retraining, relocation support and housing availability
Cut interest rates to boost demand
choices.feedback: Demand is not the binding constraint; the mismatch is.

choices.label: Wait for search to clear the market
choices.feedback: The China-shock evidence shows adjustment taking a decade or more.

supply.text: Supply-side matching policy. The China-shock evidence shows the cost is concentrated and persistent, so scale and patience matter — aggregate gains from trade are real but not evenly shared.

demand.text: Demand stimulus cannot relocate a worker or retrain a miner; it may overheat the region that already has jobs.

cyc.text: Cyclical unemployment is the recession share; here the jobs are not coming back with demand — the mismatch is structural.

fric.text: Frictional unemployment is weeks of search, not a decade of depressed participation.

wait.text: Search frictions do not explain a decade of depressed participation; the mismatch is structural.

config.why: Structural unemployment is diagnosed by duration and mismatch and treated with supply-side matching policy; the China shock shows how long the adjustment can take.

activities.anchor: One worked country-day shows the dashboard in motion
activities.caption: mark the unemployment rate
activities.name: ueRatePlace

config.prompt: In the worked example, 2.7 million people are unemployed out of a 34 million labour force. Place the unemployment rate.
config.why: 2.7 ÷ 34 = 7.9%. The participation rate (34 ÷ 52 = 65%) is the number that keeps the headline honest.

activities.caption: two categories the headline blurs — drag the divider
activities.name: ueHiddenCompare

config.prompt: Two categories the headline blurs — drag the divider:

before.label: seasonal unemployment
before.text: follows the calendar — ski instructors in July, fruit pickers after harvest — smoothed by seasonally adjusted series and off-season trades

after.label: hidden unemployment
after.text: employed in name only — the underemployed part-timer, the overqualified graduate, subsistence farming with near-zero marginal product

config.why: Both sharpen the measurement lesson: the unemployment rate is a narrow gate, and the honest read pairs it with broader underutilisation measures.

activities.anchor: moderate minimums in practice raised pay
activities.caption: true or false — the minimum-wage evidence
activities.name: ueMinimumJudge

statements.s: The simple competitive model predicts that a wage floor above the market wage creates unemployment.
statements.why: A price floor above equilibrium leaves more people wanting work than firms want to hire.

statements.s: Card and Krueger's New Jersey study found large employment losses from a moderate minimum-wage rise.
statements.why: It found small employment effects — the result that forced the textbook to take monopsony seriously.

statements.s: Monopsony power can let a moderate minimum wage raise pay with little employment loss.
statements.why: An employer that already sets wages below competitive levels can absorb a moderate floor.

statements.s: The evidence supports very large minimum-wage rises as confidently as moderate ones.
statements.why: The consensus is dose-dependent: small rises, small costs; very large rises, untested.
